content: Trichomonas vaginalis is a common cause of vaginitis and is one of the most prevalent sexually transmitted infections. This condition can also affect women during pregnancy. However, it remains uncertain whether trichomoniasis directly contributes to preterm birth or other complications during pregnancy. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of different treatments for trichomoniasis in pregnant women. To achieve this, a search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register as of January 14, 2011. The review included randomized controlled trials that compared anti-trichomonas treatments in pregnant women, regardless of whether they were symptomatic or asymptomatic. Two authors independently assessed the eligibility and quality of the trials. Ultimately, two trials involving a total of 842 pregnant women were included in the analysis. In both studies, approximately 90% of the women achieved parasitological clearance of trichomonas from the vagina following treatment. In one trial conducted in the United States, asymptomatic pregnant women between 16 and 23 weeks of gestation were treated with metronidazole on two separate occasions, at least two weeks apart. However, this trial was terminated early because metronidazole did not reduce the risk of preterm birth and was associated with a potential increase in harm. Specifically, the risk ratio for preterm birth was 1.78, with a 95% confidence interval ranging from 1.19 to 2.66, indicating a statistically significant increase in risk. The second trial, conducted in South Africa, enrolled women later in their pregnancies. However, this study lacked the design and statistical power to adequately assess adverse clinical outcomes related to the treatment. Two additional studies identified during the most recent update were excluded because they did not address the primary research question. In conclusion, metronidazole, when administered as a single dose, appears to be effective in achieving parasitological cure for trichomoniasis. However, it remains unclear whether this treatment has any beneficial impact on pregnancy outcomes. The cure rate for trichomoniasis might be improved if sexual partners of the affected women also receive treatment.
